title: How the platform fits together
kicker: Architecture, from the owner’s first upload to playback
summary: Domain boundaries, durable hand-offs, worker paths and trade-offs of Media and Processing.
opening_answer: Media owns people, uploads and playback access; Processing owns jobs and encoding attempts. They coordinate through versioned messages, each on its own database cluster. A worker (Lambda for short clips, Fargate otherwise) turns a pinned source version into outputs; Media exposes them only to the owner.
takeaways: Media owns the Asset and a copy of Processing status; Processing owns Job, Attempt and output descriptors, each on its own Aurora cluster.
SQL is authoritative. Queues wake consumers; outbox, inbox, repair and version fences cover duplicate, delayed or missing messages.
Uploads go straight to versioned S3; the verified version is pinned before work is accepted.
Clips of 60 s, 64 MiB and 1080p or less encode on Lambda; others on finite Fargate encoders (cap 3).
Playback needs ownership and projection checks, not just a finished encode.
The old `app` package is not the current runtime.

sections.title: Start with the work the system promises

blocks.text: An owner submits a video, asks for a change, and later watches the result. The visible item is an **Asset**, owned by one account; its ID is also the public job ID.
An Asset has one Processing **Job** with numbered **Attempts**. A retry makes a new attempt from the accepted source, so we know which try failed and which output belongs to which.

blocks.q: Why are Job and Attempt separate?
blocks.a: A job is the requested processing; an attempt is one execution. A retry is new work without erasing failure history or mixing outputs.

sections.title: Two owners, with a deliberate seam

blocks.text: **Media** owns accounts, ownership checks, upload reservations, pinned sources, job reads, playback signing, deletion and cleanup. **Processing** owns jobs, attempts, leases, retries, cancellation, output records and encoder claims.

Each service has its own Aurora cluster, database and role: Media `media_db` (original), Processing `processing_db` (copy-on-write clone; AD-29, #94). No cross-database joins or shared ORM models; IDs crossing the seam are contract values. Both auto-pause at 0 ACU.

blocks.text: Media keeps a `ProcessingProjection`, a local read model of the latest accepted Processing state, so status reads never touch Processing’s database. Before the first result it shows `accepted`, which Processing never emits.

blocks.text: Identity and playback stay in Media: those rules need owner and Asset together.

blocks.q: Is the Media authorizer a third service?
blocks.a: No. It is an execution role running Media code over Media’s user records. Boundaries follow owned rules, data and release units.

sections.title: From client bytes to an accepted command

blocks.text: The client requests a reservation (request key, filename, content type, byte length, SHA-256). Media returns a short-lived presigned POST for a server-chosen, owner-scoped S3 key. Bytes go straight to S3, never through API Gateway or Lambda.

`finalize` verifies size, checksum, media signature and S3 VersionId outside SQL locks. One transaction then records the VersionId, creates the Asset and stages a `submit` message: the accepted source is the version Media checked.

spec.caption: A missing or changed upload is rejected before it becomes work.

blocks.text: Cost: the client hashes first; abandoned writes need cleanup. Benefit: the worker reads exactly the accepted bytes. Repeats are safe: the same request key returns the accepted item; with different data it conflicts.

blocks.q: What if S3 has no object when finalize runs?
blocks.a: No Asset is created and nothing is enqueued: a recoverable client error.

sections.title: Messages carry work across the seam

blocks.text: Services never call each other synchronously to create a job. Media writes an outbox row beside the Asset change; a repair publisher sends it to `processing-commands`. Processing records it in its inbox, creates Job and Attempt, and stages work for `processing-work`. Snapshots return on `media-results` and update the projection.
Outbox: a commit and an SQS send cannot be atomic, so state and send-intent commit together and a publisher retries; a claim token stops a stale publisher acknowledging a row it no longer owns.

Standard SQS delivers at least once and can reorder. The inbox stores message ID and body hash in the domain transaction: same ID and body is a no-op, same ID with different content a conflict. Repair rebuilds lost work from SQL. Recoverable, not exactly once.

A per-Asset `SubmissionGuard` serializes submit, retry and cancel. Snapshots carry increasing `state_version` and attempt identity; Media ignores older versions, rejects conflicts and refuses outputs outside the job/attempt path.

blocks.q: Does inbox deduplication mean exactly-once processing?
blocks.a: No. Repeated delivery of an ID and body is harmless, but delivery can still repeat and repair still covers the SQL-to-queue gap.

sections.title: From a worker lease to owner playback

blocks.text: A worker asks Processing to claim the Job and Attempt. Processing checks source, owner and Asset identity, current attempt, submission guard and finite task binding, then issues a lease token on the database clock; heartbeat and finish must present it before the deadline.

The worker downloads the pinned source, probes, validates edits and runs FFmpeg. Outputs go under `jobs/{job_id}/attempts/{attempt_id}/`: one primary output, HLS optional. Terminal state commits before the SQS message is deleted. A worker that loses its lease is fenced out; a retry makes a new Attempt.

spec.caption: Benchmark sl1021: queue wait 0.26 s vs 32.6 s Fargate; processing 5.3 s vs 8.0 s; submit to done 45.2 s warm, 92.0 s cold vs 87.7 s; $0.0003 vs $0.0021 per encode; 5 jobs/arm, 0 failures. 35-80 s unexplained: 20 s target still missed (AWS page).

blocks.text: Media accepts a result only if the source matches its pin and output keys belong to the attempt, after version and attempt fences. MP4: owner check, then a short-lived signed S3 URL. HLS: private uncached playlist, segments redirected to signed URLs. A foreign owner or unknown Asset looks not found.

spec.title: Work becomes playback
spec.caption: Projection validation and owner authorization make playback safe.

blocks.text: Failure example: attempt 1 stalls, the owner retries, attempt 2 starts. Worker 1 waking later fails the lease check; a late result fails the attempt number and state version. Its output stays under attempt 1.

blocks.q: Why can a signed link expire?
blocks.a: It is a short-lived capability to read one output; a fresh owner-authorized read mints another. No permanent public object URL exists.

sections.title: Know the boundaries and the trade-offs

blocks.text: Separate clusters and IAM roles limit coordination but share the account, VPC and queues. Media can hold a command while Processing is down; encoding waits for capacity. V1: bounded batches started by a person. V2-live: launcher wakes finite Fargate tasks (cap 3); short clips use Lambda. Neither is always-on.
The Publisher CLI is an integrator: public HTTPS only, no application, database or storage imports. `contracts/` is the message language between images.

Root `app/` and `app/worker/` are the earlier Redis/RQ monolith. Current paths: `media/`, `processing/`, `contracts/`, `delivery/`, `runtime_support/`. Current design: SQS, SQL outbox/inbox, finite workers.

Design test: does an abstraction protect a real invariant, boundary or repeated policy? Repositories centralize owner-filtered SQL, services compose actions, adapters hold transport, contracts define boundary values. Pass-through wrappers, a service per noun or a generic workflow engine only add navigation.
